label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
reason: formatting, assistant talk or a placeholder
output:
Here it is. I kept the anger in it but held it together, so it reads like a person who is very upset and very serious — not like someone who wants a fight. Send it as written, then stop looking at your phone and wait for him to call.

---

**Subject: The building on Saint-Hubert — please call me today**

Denis,

I'm writing this because I can't say all of this to you right now without losing my temper, and you deserve to hear every word of it, not the version an agent gives you on the way out the door. So I'm going to write it out long, the way it came out of my head, and then I'm going to ask you to call me. You. Not your wife. Not a text she types for you. Me.

Last Thursday at 6 in the morning, a photographer from the agency walked into my bakery while I was shaping baguettes. He had a camera. He told me that you had already said it was fine with me, that I was okay with it, that I knew about it.

I was standing at my bench with the oven already hot and I didn't understand what he was saying. For about ten seconds I thought I was still asleep. Then I had to go and put the baguettes in, because if I didn't put the baguettes in I was going to fall apart right there in front of him. And then Karine had to calm me down. My employee, Karine, who has worked with me for eleven years, had to be the one holding me together while I was standing in my own shop. In the shop my father built.

I'm not telling you this so you feel bad. I'm telling you this so you know what it did to me. Because I found out the biggest thing that has happened to my life in the last two years, from a stranger with a camera, at six in the morning, while I was working. I found out my brother was selling our father's building and I found out from a man who took photographs of my ovens.

You didn't even call me. You used an agent to tell me, because it's easier that way. I keep thinking about that and I can't get past it. You were in Calgary, you had a phone, your phone works. You called me after maman's funeral. You could have called me on Thursday. Instead you sent a man with a camera into my bakery to do it for you.

Now let me tell you about the building, because I don't think you have been looking at it the way I have been looking at it every single day.

Three floors on rue Saint-Hubert. Papa bought it in 1979. The bakery downstairs, two apartments up. That is where I have baked since I was twenty-six years old. That's thirty-one years. That's my whole life.

Since maman died in February, the building is half yours and half mine. The estate was settled in August. I pay $2,400 a month in rent to the estate and I have never been late, not once, not one single month. I have paid my share every month like a clock. And in 2019 I paid for the new roof myself. $38,000, my own money, and I did not ask anybody to split it and nobody was going to. I did it because the roof was going to fall in on the bakery and the bakery is the only thing I know how to keep alive. So do the math if you want, Denis. You can add up what I have put into that building since 1979 and compare it to what you have put into it, and then look me in the face and tell me again that I'm the sentimental one.

The listing came up at $1,150,000 with an agent, and I found it on Centris like everybody else in Montreal. That is what it feels like to be on the other side of this, by the way. You put a sign on it and I found it the same way a stranger would.

Here is what I have been working on, and what I have already told you. In September, by phone, I told you that I wanted to buy your half of the building. The caisse has pre-approved me for $410,000. I have a pre-approval letter. I am not asking you for a gift, I am not asking you for the building to stay in the family out of kindness. I am offering you money for your half, real money, through a real mortgage, and I have told you about it already, on the phone, in September, so that this would not be a surprise to you in December.

And then you called me after maman's funeral, and you said to me, "No rush, we decide together." Together. You said that to me standing next to our mother's grave, and three weeks later the sign went up. I have replayed that conversation about a hundred times. I keep waiting for the part where you explain it to me.

And here's the part that makes me the most furious, so please hear it. You think I want this because I am sentimental. I do love that building. I love it the way you loved sleeping in the flour sacks in the back room when we were kids, remember, when Papa let you have that room because you loved it so much, and you would tell everybody you were sleeping in a bakery. I remember that. I have never forgotten it. But Denis, this is business too. This is six employees who depend on me. This is thirty-one years of clients, families, people who come in on Saturday morning and buy bread from the same woman for three decades. If a developer buys that building, he will tear it down or he will turn it into condos, and my rent will double, and I cannot survive a doubled rent. Not financially, not emotionally, not for one more year. I would have to close. I would have to close the bakery that Papa's building has housed since before you and I were born.

So what happens if you sell? What happens to me is I lose my lease in a building that is half mine anyway, in a neighbourhood where I cannot afford what I would then need to pay, and I lose my brother's respect at the same time. That is what happens. You can go to Calgary and be the guy whose sister lost her bakery.

I am not asking you to do this for the family. I am asking you to do this because it is the fair thing and because I have earned it.

So here is what I want, and I want it this week:

One — take it off the market. Pull the listing.

Two — if you will not pull it, then give me the first right to buy, in writing, for my offer, at terms we agree on, with the building not shown to anybody else before you have heard my answer. I have a pre-approval for $410,000 and I can move quickly on the rest. I have been ready since September. I have been ready for three months while you were saying "no rush."

I know my lease finishes on 30 April 2027. That is the other reason I cannot let this sit. Every month this goes on, I am a tenant in a building I co-own, paying rent to an estate, while my brother negotiates with agents behind my back. I need to know where I stand before then, not after.

And please — please — the answer comes to me by phone. I don't want a text from your wife telling me that you are "working on it" or that you will "call later." I want to hear your voice. I want to hear you say the words yourself, whatever the words are. If you have something to tell me, if you think I'm wrong about the money, if you think the developer is offering something better than what I can give, then say it to my face and I will listen to all of it. I will even listen to you tell me that I am being dramatic, because at least then we are having the conversation like brother and sister instead of you and an agent and a photographer with a camera.

I am angry, Denis. I want you to feel it. Do not read this and think I am calm and reasonable and just being cautious. I am furious that I found out the way I found out, and I am hurt in a way I did not expect to be hurt by you. But I am not writing to you to punish you and I am not writing to you to cut you out. I don't want to lose my brother. I don't want to end up at fifty-eight with no brother and no bakery and nothing of Papa's left. I would rather lose money than lose you. But I am not going to lose both, and that is exactly what is on the table right now.

Call me today. Today, Denis. I am at the bakery from 5 in the morning, so call the shop any time before nine or call me at home after seven. I will pick up.

I am waiting.

Your sister,
[Name]

---

**One small suggestion:** if you want to make it even harder to ignore, add one line at the very top under the subject, before the first paragraph: *"Please read this to the end before you do anything else, and then call me."* It stops him from skimming the first three paragraphs and calling your wife instead.
